messages.body_plain:
I've actually read this paper before.

2 items per factor is kind of rough, but in this case it is identifiable because of items you have. If you were to just model that one factor without the rest of the items in the correlation matrix, you'd have to constrain more parameters in the model. You also may not have very high reliability on this particular factor (I would use multidimensional omega in this case, in the paper you cite they call it composite reliability - they cite Fornell & Larcker, I would also cite Raykov and MacDonald). I'd also point out that the ct2 factor only has 2 as well.

It is interesting that your model doesn't track that close to their model on all of the factors. If your data were collected in a high quality fashion and the instrument was the same as what they used, then this would be an interesting finding worthy of publication I think. You may even want to communicate with the authors, maybe they can provide some insight as to why your model is different. Your model fit - though not great - isn't that far of what is reported in the paper, and if you remove a6 it is better than what they reported.

Regarding your comment about the the 0.3 cutoff for relevant items - I think that is relative to your model. If your loadings are well higher than that, then a6 loading at 0.3 seems like it doesn't belong. Given the high mod index, I think you are justified from a statistical standpoint in removing it. From the conceptual side, it may be necessary to keep that item in your model, but in that case I would consider reworking it into your model better. Remember, just because model fit has numbers doesn't mean that is all you need to consider. Model fit is only as good as the models you compare it to.

A couple things you may want to think about: explore correlations among residuals. This would violate local independence, and indicate that there may be something else going on, perhaps another factor or some cross-loadings. Keep in mind, cross-loadings may or may not be acceptable depending on what you are trying to do. Based on how this paper uses the F&L framework for divergent/convergent validity among the factors, it looks like that isn't something you would want.

You also have some items with low loadings: a6 loads under 0.3 on ct1. These are going to be signs that you have parameters that are not "correctly" specified. You'll notice the first 3 modindices all pertain to item a6, which has that low loading. The epc for the mod on dm, and negative for the mods on as and ct2.
> >

> > inspect(fitcfa1,"coef")$psi
> >
> > Obtains negative relationships between dm and ct2 and as. Right now a6 loads low on ct1, which has a positive correlation with dm, none with ct1, and positive with as. This correlation structure looks a little odd - and could be driven by the misplacement of a6.
> >
> > Look what happens when you respecify the model following the modindices - make a6 load on ct2 and as. Fit stats are slightly better (though not drastically); a6 still loads low on the two other factors, so again you may want to adjust. > On 03/31/2014 01:17 PM, Jeffrey Henry wrote:
> > Dear all,
> >
> > I would like to know relevant syntax specifications and/or R packages I
> > should download to produce a marginal maximum likelihood (MML) estimator
> > in a confirmatory factor analysis (CFA).
>
> I'm not sure what you are asking for. Syntax? Nothing special, just
> describe your model as usual. To use MML, simply add estimator="MML" to
> the cfa/sem/lavaan call.
>
> For example:
>
> # create binary data
> HS9 <-
> HolzingerSwineford1939[,c("x1","x2","x3","x4","x5","x6","x7","x8","x9")]
> HSbinary <- as.data.frame( lapply(HS9, cut, 2, labels=FALSE) )
>
> # describe model (here a one-dimensional cfa)
> model <- ' trait =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + x5 + x6 + x7 + x8 + x9 '
>
> # fit model
> fit <- cfa(model, data=HSbinary, ordered=names(HSbinary), std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE,
> estimator="MML")
>
> # look at results
> summary(fit)
>
>
> Other R packages? Look at the 'mirt' package. Which is currently much,
> much faster (using C++), but MML only.
>
> References? Try anything with 'IRT'.
>
> Some books:
>
> van der Linden, W. J., & Hambleton, R. K. (Eds.). (1997). Handbook of
> modern item response theory. New York, NY: Springer.
>
> Hambleton, R.K., and Swaminathan, H. Item Response Theory: Principles
> and Applications. Hingham, MA: Kluwer, Nijhoff, 1984.
>
> Skrondal, A., & Rabe-Hesketh, S. (2004). Generalized latent variable
> modeling: Multilevel, longitudinal, and structural equation models. CRC
> Press.
>
> Bartholomew, D. J., Knott, M., & Moustaki, I. (2011). Latent variable
> models and factor analysis: a unified approach (Vol. 899). John Wiley &
> Sons.
>
> Yves.

             Y ~ b*M
           # indirect effect (a*b)
             ab := a*b
           # total effect
             total := c + (a*b)'
fit <- sem(model, data = Data)
summary(fit)
Regards,

messages.body_plain:
On 04/04/2014 06:45 AM, Mike Cheung wrote:
> Dear Oscar,
>
> Thanks for your reply. It is not in this case. Since "ab" and "total"
> are not parameters in the model, vcov() does not work. I can obtain it
> by using the delta method. Since lavaan has already implemented it the
> delta method to obtain the SEs, I wonder whether I can get the full matrix.

I am afraid not (yet).

You can do it manually, using some internal functions, like this:

set.seed(1234)
X <- rnorm(100)
M <- 0.5*X + rnorm(100)
Y <- 0.7*M + rnorm(100)
Data <- data.frame(X = X, Y = Y, M = M)
model <- ' # direct effect
              Y ~ c*X
            # mediator
              M ~ a*X
              Y ~ b*M
            # indirect effect (a*b)
              ab := a*b
            # total effect
              total := c + (a*b)'
fit <- sem(model, data = Data)

# first get ordinary vcov
VCOV <- vcov(fit)

# extract free parameters
x <- fit@Fit@x

# compute jacobian for 'defined parameters'
JAC <- lavaan:::lavJacobianD(func = fit@Mod...@def.function, x = x)

# vcov for defined parameters, using delta method
VCOV.def <- JAC %*% VCOV %*% t(JAC)

If you need the 'full' vcov, just combine VCOV and VCOV.def in a block
diagonal matrix:

lavaan:::bdiag(VCOV, VCOV.def)

But lavaan should return this out of the box. I will add this to my TODO
list.

Yves.

Local independence ive seen most often brought up in the context of item response theory or rasch modeling - if you google that im sure you can find all sorts of resources and explanations as to why it is important from a measurement perspective.

To test for local independence you can look at the correlations of all items, not just those that losd on the same factor. Think about them differently as you evaluate the output. If residuals across different factors are correlated that means you may have an item that should load on more than one factor (and the mod index should point that out as well). If thats the case you could have a discrimant validity issue- your model doesnt cleanly differentiate among the factors because your items are cross loading. Not everyone sees this as a problem but rasch modelers probably would. If you have correlated residuals of items in the sames factor that is whewre local independence is violated - that means there is something going on with those items that is not shared with the other items.

As you assess the correlations look at both statistical significance and magnitude. Depending on your sample size they could all come up as significant, but they may be too small to worry about. I dont really know how sample size in an ordinal cfa plays in to the residual estimation so i cant really comment on the specifics of that aspect.

> model.type = "sem",  :

Something is wrong with 'semo'. This has nothing to do with the estimator.

> Q-3 when using estimator "DWLS" . are weights are variances???

The weight matrix (the 'W' in WLS) is the inverse of the asymptotic
variance matrix of the sample statistics (thresholds, polychorics). See
muthen (1984) for the theory.

> Q-4 are they WLSM, WLSMVS, WLSMV robust estimates for DWLS.?

estimator="WLSMV" implies:
1) estimator="DWLS"
2) se="robust"
3) test="scaled.shifted"

WLSMVS only affects the test to the 'old' mean and variance
Satterthwaite correction:

1) estimator="DWLS"
2) se="robust"
3) test="mean.var.adjusted"

WLSM only affects the test, using the mean-adjustment only (aka Satorra
Bentler)

1) estimator="DWLS"
2) se="robust"
3) test="satorra.bentler"

WLS implies:

1) estimator="WLS"
2) se="standard"
3) test="standard"

Yves

messages.body_plain:
On 04/01/2014 03:33 PM, Jeffrey Henry wrote:
> Thanks for taking the time. Here it is. It is a big syntax, but quite
> simple really. All items load on a general factor + their respective,
> uncorrelated subfactors. Each factor is represented twice. For example,
> CU1 = twin 1, and CU2 = twin 2. The same goes for the observed
> variables, assessed for both twins 1 and 2. There are also other minor
> specifications (e.g., equality constraints on observed variables'
> intercepts, equality constraints in factor loadings from family (twin 1,
> twin 2) and zygosity group (MZ, DZ)); see the Olsen and Kelly paper
> attached in my other message). Grouping is made according to zygosity
> (Group 1 = MZ; Group 2 = DZ).

Are the indicators categorical (binary/ordered)?

If yes, so need to specify the thresholds in the syntax (or use the
sem() function instead of the lavaan() function if you are unsure which
parameters are needed; or use the auto.th <http://auto.th>=TRUE flag in the lavaan()
function). Also, categorical indicators do not have 'free' residual
variances (at least not under the default 'delta'  parameterization), so
you can not impose equality constraints on them. You might consider
parameterization="theta" instead. Intercepts are also not needed, since
you have thresholds (which you may constrain to be equal across groups).

If no, and all your data is continuous, please use estimator="ML".
Estimator MML currently (0.5-16) only works for categorical data. And
for continuous data, MML == ML.

Yves.

AIC = -2 * logl + 2*npar

where 'logl' is the loglikelihood of the model, and 'npar' is the number
of free parameters.

BIC = -2 * logl + npar*log(N)

where N is the total sample size.

To get the ingredients from a fitted lavaan object ('fit'), so can use:

fitMeasures(fit, "logl")   # or logLik(fit)
fitMeasures(fit, "npar")
fitMeasures(fit, "ntotal") # or nobs(fit)

Yves.

Hello,
I've been using AMOS to compute the composite reliability of a number of cognitive tasks and I'd like to learn how to do the same thing using lavaan.
Composite reliability as discussed by Raykov (1997) is estimated in an SEM model, where the factor indicators are simultaneously predicted by a general factor (T) and predictive of another latent factor (X) that approximates the total observed score - this is referred to as a phantom variable. Composite reliability is thus the correlation (or squared correlation) between T (the true score) and X (the observed score). This correlation between T and X is not indicated in the model but rather is obtained via an "implied" correlation matrix consisting of all latent/observed variables in the model.

model1='

t =~ 1*x1 + x2 + x3 + x4
'

My question is: is the lavaan model misspecified in any obvious ways? And if not, what is the cause of the error?

I should mention that I was able to obtain the implied correlation matrix despite this error and it matches the AMOS estimates within .001 difference, which is excellent.

Assuming these are all observed variable, you need to create a product term in your data frame first (e.g., dat$IT <- dat$EX1 * dat$EX2), then enter it as another exogenous predictor in your model.  If you are using "fixed.x = TRUE" then you don't need to include the covariances between IT and EX1 or EX2 because those parameters won't be estimated, but taken directly from the data summary (implicitly, they will be allowed to correlate).

messages.body_plain:
>
> I have two latent variables that are made up of ordinal indicators. I'm trying to see how these two latent variables correlate to my measured variables. However, I kept receiving errors when using lavaan. These errors disappear if I define regressions instead of correlations (i.e. "SV + FM + EF ~ CN + AM").

lavaan uses LISREL matrices to represent the model, and there is no matrix for covariances between latent and observed variables.  When you regress the observed outcomes on latent variables, it works because behind the scenes, lavaan creates single-indicator constructs from the observed outcomes, and regresses the "latent" constructs (SV + FM + EF) on the latent predictors (CN + AM).  I suppose a similar automated mechanism is not in place when you try to covary observed and latent variables.  But you can do so in your syntax:

model <- '
  CN =~ N1 + N3 + N6 + G13 + G7 + G5

  AM =~N2 + N4 + G16

## create single-indicator constructs to put observed variables in latent space
  SV.lat =~ SV  ## the sem() function automatically fixes residual
  FM.lat =~ FM  ## the variance of single-indicator construct to 0
  EF.lat =~ EF
## covary them
  SV.lat + FM.lat + EF.lat ~~ CN + AM '

Terry

messages.subject_clean: what is the definition of an interaction term between two exogenous variables?
messages.body_plain:
I think that it is an excellent question.  This (direct effects with interaction) is not my area of expertise--I don't know what the literature says.  But, if I reason from a regression perspective, the interaction means that the effect of A and the effect of B depend on the value of the other variable.  So a generalized statement about "the effect of A" no longer makes sense.  You can now only calculate the effect of A for a certain value of B, and vice versa.  If you specify a value of B (like its mean), then you can compute simple slopes (consult a good regression text, like Cohen, Cohen, West and Aiken [2003]) and, from that, calculate the quantity that you want.  Once you get simple slopes, then you have already accounted for the interaction term.  You can plug the simple slope results into your path model and do the calculations.
     The literature may have another viw, but that's mine.
--Ed Rigdon

If you are using WLSMV (which is the default in both Mplus and lavaan
when data is categorical), then the default setting for the test
argument (test = "scaled.shifed") should reproduce the chi-square value
of Mplus very closely. If not, let me know.

The difference can only be seen if you are using DIFFTEST in Mplus, to
compare two nested models.

> Could you please give me a hint on how to set thresholds equal across
> groups?

The 'group.equal' argument can be used for this. For example, you can use

fit <- cfa(myModel, data=myData, group="Group",
group.equal=c("loadings","thresholds"), ordered=c("i1","i2",...), ...)

Or, in the syntax, you can label the thresholds. If you want different
thresholds for each group, you give them a different label, eg

i1 | c(a1, a2)*t1

If you want to constrain the thresholds to be the same across groups,
you give them the same label:

i1 | c(a1,a1)*t1

Yves.

A sum score does not remove measurement error, it only reduces the proportion of measurement error (relative to the proportion in dams, ditch, and aqueduc).  Defining a latent variable with the same observed measures should remove measurement error (if the assumption of a common underlying cause is true).

I believe specifying "WDI =~ dams + ditch + aqueduc" in your model syntax will define a latent variable "WDI" and ignore the observed variable of the same name, but it would be better to avoid confusion by deleting the sum score or by changing the name of the latent variable, e.g., "WDI.factor =~ dams + ditch + aqueduc"

Terry
